abstract: |
  Date numerology assigns one of nine planets to each civil day from the
  digit sum of the day of the month. The Moon's nakshatra lord names one of
  the same nine planets and changes about once a day. We derive analytically
  why the two labels change at unrelated instants and why their long-run
  agreement must equal chance, then test two pre-registered equivalence
  hypotheses on five years of sidereal (Lahiri) positions sampled at a fixed
  clock time: Cohen's kappa between the two labels, and the correlation of
  each planet's numerology indicator with its dignity score. The outcome,
  stated in the Summary, is generated from the pipeline's `results.json`.
keywords: [numerology, nakshatra, equivalence test, TOST, Cohen's kappa]

## Corrections {.unnumbered}

The earlier version of this paper (withdrawn 2026-11-08, see
[CORRECTIONS.md](../../../CORRECTIONS.md)) claimed "99.48% orthogonality",
about 73 numerology changes a year and a synchronisation rate
"statistically indistinguishable from chance". Those claims did not follow
from the analysis:

- the hypothesis test set `reject_null = p >= 0.05` under the null "the
  systems are correlated", so a non-significant correlation was read as
  proof of independence (review item S1-20);
- all planets were flattened into one series and correlated as if the
  pooled values were independent observations;
- "temporal stationarity" was a paired t-test on a single pair of numbers;
- positions were tropical, and the scripts built naive datetimes, which the
  corrected engine rejects, so no day could be computed;
- the "73 changes a year" was a constant typed into the script; the label
  changes at almost every midnight (@sec-derivation).

This version replaces the independence claim with TOST equivalence tests
against margins fixed in `hypothesis.yaml` before the run, and states the
temporal argument as a derivation.

# The two labels

**Numerology planet.** For a civil date with day of month $d$ the mulanka
is the digital root $r(d) = 1 + (d - 1) \bmod 9$, mapped to a planet:
1 Sun, 2 Moon, 3 Jupiter, 4 Rahu, 5 Mercury, 6 Venus, 7 Ketu, 8 Saturn,
9 Mars. The label depends only on the date, not on the time of day or on
any position.

**Moon's nakshatra lord.** The sidereal ecliptic is divided into 27
nakshatras of $13^\circ 20'$; nakshatra $k = \lfloor \lambda_{\text{Moon}} /
13^\circ 20' \rfloor$ has the Vimshottari lord $L(k \bmod 9)$ in the order
Ketu, Venus, Sun, Moon, Mars, Rahu, Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury. Each lord rules
three nakshatras $120^\circ$ apart.

# Why the two labels cannot be synchronised {#sec-derivation}

**Numerology changes at civil midnight, and almost every midnight.**
Consecutive integers have different digital roots, so $r(d+1) \neq r(d)$
within a month. Across a month end $r$ returns to $r(1) = 1$ from $r(31) =
4$, $r(30) = 3$, $r(29) = 2$ or $r(28) = 1$: only 28 February to 1 March in
a common year leaves the label unchanged. The label therefore changes at
364 of 365 midnights in a common year and at all 366 in a leap year, always
exactly at midnight in the chosen zone. Over a year the digital roots 1-4
occur on 4 days of most months and 5-9 on 3, so the Sun, Moon, Jupiter and
Rahu are numerology planets slightly more often than the other five.

**The nakshatra lord changes at instants set by the Moon.** The Moon's mean
sidereal motion is $360^\circ / 27.3217\,\text{d} = 13.18^\circ$ a day, so it
spends on average $27.3217 / 27 = 1.012$ days in a nakshatra (between about
0.87 and 1.13 days as its speed varies from about $11.8^\circ$ to
$15.4^\circ$ a day). The boundary crossings fall at clock times fixed by the
Moon's longitude, not by the calendar. Because the sidereal month is not a
rational multiple of the solar day, those crossing times are, in the long
run, uniformly distributed over the 24 hours. On almost every civil day the
lord changes at some hour, so a date-based label cannot correspond to a
single nakshatra lord: which lord a day "has" depends on the hour at which
it is read.

**Long-run agreement equals chance.** The day of the month cycles with the
civil calendar (28-31 days) while the nakshatra index cycles with the
sidereal month (27.32 days). These periods are incommensurate, so by
equidistribution the long-run joint frequency of (numerology planet $i$,
lord $j$) factorises into $p_N(i)\,p_M(j)$. Each lord rules 120 degrees of
longitude, so $p_M(j) \to 1/9$, and the expected agreement is
$$\sum_i p_N(i)\,p_M(i) = \tfrac{1}{9} \sum_i p_N(i) = \tfrac{1}{9}$$
whatever the numerology frequencies are. Cohen's kappa
$\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)$ therefore tends to 0. Over a finite period
the observed agreement fluctuates around $1/9$ with a width set by the
number of independent lunar cycles in the sample.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| label: tbl-derivation
#| tbl-cap: "Derived and observed quantities over the sample period."

rows = [
    ("Numerology label changes per year", "364-366",
     f(D["numerology_changes_per_year"], 1)),
    ("Mean days per nakshatra", "1.012", f(D["mean_nakshatra_days"], 3)),
    ("Nakshatra-lord changes between daily samples, per year",
     "about 350: 365 less the intervals inside a nakshatra longer than a day",
     f(D["nakshatra_lord_changes_per_year"], 1)),
    ("Share of days per nakshatra lord", "1/9 = 0.111",
     f"{min(D['nakshatra_lord_share'].values()):.3f} to "
     f"{max(D['nakshatra_lord_share'].values()):.3f}"),
    ("Expected agreement from the margins", "1/9 = 0.111",
     f(D["chance_agreement_from_margins"], 4)),
]
print("| Quantity | Derived | Observed |")
```

# Pre-registered tests

The study file `hypothesis.yaml` (registered 2026-11-08, before the first run
of the corrected pipeline) fixes the period, the sampling moment and two
hypotheses. A non-significant test cannot show that two series are
unrelated; equivalence is shown with two one-sided tests (TOST) that the
estimate lies above the lower margin and below the upper margin, which is
the same as its 90% confidence interval lying inside the margin.

- **H1.** Cohen's kappa between the numerology planet and the Moon's
  nakshatra lord lies within $(-0.05, 0.05)$.
- **H2.** For each of the nine planets, the correlation between the
  numerology indicator (1 on days the planet rules, 0 otherwise) and that
  planet's dignity score lies within $(-0.10, 0.10)$, tested on the Fisher
  $z$ scale. Each planet is its own claim, so no multiplicity correction is
  applied.

Consecutive days are dependent, so standard errors come from a stationary
block bootstrap with a mean block of 27 days (about one sidereal month),
2,000 resamples, seed 42. For kappa the larger of the bootstrap and the
Fleiss-Cohen-Everitt asymptotic standard error is used. The functions are
`tost` and `cohen_kappa_ci` in `vedic_astrology_core.stats.equivalence`.

# Results

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| label: tbl-kappa
#| tbl-cap: "H1: agreement between the numerology planet and the Moon's nakshatra lord."
print("| Quantity | Value |")

print(f"| Days | {K['n']:,} |")
print(f"| Observed agreement | {f(K['observed_agreement'], 4)} |")
print(f"| Expected agreement | {f(K['expected_agreement'], 4)} |")
print(f"| Cohen's kappa | {f(K['kappa'], 4)} |")
print(f"| SE (asymptotic / block bootstrap) | {f(K['se_analytic'], 4)} / "
      f"{f(K['se_bootstrap'], 4)} |")
print(f"| 90% CI | {f(K['ci90_tost'][0], 4)} to {f(K['ci90_tost'][1], 4)} |")
print(f"| Margin | +-{K['margin_kappa']} |")
print(f"| TOST p | {pval(K['p_tost'])} |")
print(f"| Equivalent | {'yes' if K['equivalent'] else 'not shown'} |")
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| label: tbl-planets
#| tbl-cap: "H2: correlation of each planet's numerology indicator with its dignity score."
print("| Planet | r | 90% CI | TOST p | Equivalent |")

for p in P:
    if "r" not in p:
        print(f"| {p['planet']} | - | - | - | {p['skipped']} |")

    print(f"| {p['planet']} | {f(p['r'], 4)} | {f(p['r_ci90_low'], 3)} to "
          f"{f(p['r_ci90_high'], 3)} | {pval(p['p_tost'])} | "
          f"{'yes' if p['equivalent'] else 'not shown'} |")
```

# Limitations

```{python}
#| output: asis
model = RES["ephemeris"].get("ephemeris_model")
print(f"""
- H1 is close to a consistency check: @sec-derivation shows that kappa must
  tend to zero for any numerology frequencies, so equivalence confirms the
  derivation and the corrected engine rather than adding new evidence.
- The margins (0.05 for kappa, 0.10 for r) were chosen by us; a smaller
  margin needs a longer period.
- One numerology convention is used (day of the civil month, no sunrise
  correction) and one sampling moment ({S['time']} {S['tz']}). Another fixed
  moment shifts which lord is read on each day but not the long-run
  argument.
- Dignity scores come from this repository's `DignityScorer`; another
  scoring model could correlate differently with the numerology indicator.
- Positions use the Swiss Ephemeris with `ephemeris_model = {model}`; the
  Moshier analytic theory is far more precise than the one-day resolution
  needed here.
""")
```
